subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Basic Unit of Change on a Blockchain
lesson.summary: A transaction is a signed, structured record of a single change to the ledger, such as a transfer of value or a call to a program, and it is the fundamental unit that blocks are built out of.
lesson.body:
Everything discussed so far in this chapter, blocks, headers, the genesis block, describes the container. This section is about what actually goes inside it. A transaction is the basic unit of change on a blockchain: a discrete, self-contained instruction, typically something like "move this amount of value from this account to that account," that a user submits to the network to be included in a future block.

This directly extends the blockchain definition covered earlier: a blockchain was described as an append-only, cryptographically linked record, but a record of what, exactly. Transactions are the answer. A block's body, discussed in the block structure section, is essentially a batch of transactions bundled together and time stamped as a group, in the order the network agreed to accept them.

A transaction typically contains a handful of essential fields: information identifying the sender, information identifying the recipient, the amount or data being transferred, and, importantly, a digital signature proving the sender authorized it, a topic explored fully in the next section on transaction validation. Some blockchains, Bitcoin among them, track ownership through a model where each transaction consumes previous "unspent" outputs as its inputs and creates new outputs, a bit like paying with a twenty dollar bill and receiving change back, rather than simply debiting and crediting an account balance directly. Other blockchains, Ethereum among them, use a more familiar account balance model, where a transaction directly increases one account's balance and decreases another's.

A concrete example clarifies the shape of the thing. Suppose Priya wants to send 2 units of a cryptocurrency to Jamal. She constructs a transaction specifying her address as the source, Jamal's address as the destination, the amount, and a small fee to compensate whoever includes her transaction in a block. She signs this transaction with her private key, broadcasts it to the network, and it sits in a pool of pending, unconfirmed transactions until a node building the next block selects it, along with others, and includes it in that block's body. Once that block is accepted by the network and, per the immutability discussion earlier, buried under enough subsequent blocks, Priya's transaction becomes a permanent, essentially unchangeable part of the ledger's history.

It is worth noting that not all blockchain transactions move currency. On networks that support smart contracts, a transaction can also be an instruction to execute code: deploying a new contract, calling a function on an existing one, or updating some piece of on-chain state. The common thread across all of these is not what changes, but the format: a discrete, signed, submitted instruction that the network as a whole must agree to accept, order, and record before it becomes real.
